title: Age-predicted maximal heart rate in healthy subjects: The HUNT Fitness Study
authors: Nes BM, Janszky I, Wisloff U, Stoylen A, Karlsen T
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
population: 3320 healthy Norwegian men and women across a wide age range with verified maximal effort (HUNT Fitness Study 2007-2008)
findings: HRmax = 211 - 0.64 x age with a standard error of the estimate (SEE) of 10.8 bpm.
No evidence of interaction with gender, physical activity, VO2max level or BMI groups; only minor age-adjusted differences between these groups.
Three previously suggested equations underestimated measured HRmax in subjects older than 30 years.
HRmax in healthy older subjects and women was higher than previously reported.
HRmax was explained by the formula 211 - 0.64 x age (SEE 10.8 bpm).
No evidence of interaction with gender, physical activity, VO2max level or BMI groups; only minor age-adjusted differences in HRmax between these groups.
Previously suggested prediction equations underestimated measured HRmax in subjects older than 30 years.
HRmax in healthy older subjects and women was higher than previously reported; the standard error of 10.8 beats/min must be taken into account.
limitations: Cross-sectional, not longitudinal; Norwegian population; lab ergometer protocol with verified maximal effort; not runner-specific. Another sample (Shookster 2020, n = 99) found this equation significantly different from measured HRmax.
implications: Use an SEE of about 10.8 bpm as the uncertainty on any age-predicted HRmax; label zones derived from a predicted HRmax as approximate and low confidence.

211 - 0.64 x age gives values about 4-7 bpm higher than 208 - 0.7 x age between ages 20 and 60 (difference widens with age); this is inside the SEE, so the choice is not critical. Prefer Tanaka as the default because Nes differed significantly from measured HRmax in Shookster 2020 while Tanaka did not.
Use 211 - 0.64 x age as a sensitivity alternative to Tanaka (it gives higher HRmax for older runners: about 6-7 bpm higher at age 60-70) and report the +/-10.8 bpm SEE.
Zones anchored on percent HRmax must be recalibrated from observed maxima, since individual HRmax can differ by 10+ bpm from any age equation.

verification.notes: Crossref: vol 23 pp 697-704, print Dec 2013, online 2012-02-29; first author Nes matches. Abstract confirms 3320, 211 - 0.64 age, SEE 10.8. Corrected the researcher's claim that the two equations 'differ little in 30-50 years': the arithmetic difference is 4.8 bpm at 30, 5.4 at 40 and 6.0 at 50 (and larger at older ages).
